strengths: Compelling and insightful core hypothesis: The paper identifies a clear and previously overlooked incompatibility in curriculum learning for LLMs—namely, that standard aggressive learning rate decay schedules (e.g., decaying to near-zero) drastically reduce update step sizes precisely when the highest-quality data is presented at the end of training.

Thorough empirical validation: The hypothesis is systematically tested across multiple LR schedules (Constant, WSD, Cosine), data orderings (Uniform, Ascend, Descend, Folding), quality scorers (DCLM fastText, PreSelect), and pretraining configurations (from-scratch, mid-training, and large-scale continual pretraining).

Practical and accessible solutions: Both proposed remedies—moderating the final LR decay ratio (WSMD) and Curriculum Model Averaging (CMA/CDMA)—are computationally cheap, straightforward to implement in production pretraining stacks, and deliver consistent improvements (up to +1.64% on downstream benchmarks without additional data filtering).

Meaningful validation scale: Beyond the 1.5B / 30B token experiments, the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of multi-domain CDMA on a 3.2B parameter model trained across >150B tokens, confirming that the insights hold in more realistic multi-domain continual pretraining settings.

Complementary theoretical formulation: The 2D stylized SGD analysis nicely formalizes the trade-off between progress along the signal direction and variance reduction along the noise direction, explaining why excessive decay fails and how weight averaging/moderate decay recovers the curriculum advantage.
weaknesses: Domain-specific regressions in multi-domain setup: In the large-scale 3.2B continual pretraining experiment (Table 10), coding performance shows a slight degradation (MBPP: -0.78) and math shows virtually no gain (GSM8K: +0.08), suggesting that simple heuristic metrics (like GitHub stars or duplication counts) and linear rank rescaling may not be optimal for specialized reasoning domains.

Heuristic cross-domain ranking assumption: The multi-domain curriculum construction (Algorithm 2) relies on uniform quantile rescaling across domains, implicitly assuming that relative quality percentiles across disparate domains (e.g., web text vs. code vs. math) correspond to equivalent absolute quality or utility.

Theoretical model is heavily stylized: The theoretical model in Section 4 is restricted to a 2D quadratic SGD setting with orthogonal signal and noise axes, which serves as a helpful conceptual intuition but does not capture non-convex optimization dynamics, momentum/Adam effects, or transformer architecture nuances.

strengths: Compelling and intuitive core insight: The paper identifies a fundamental yet widely overlooked conflict in curriculum-based LLM pretraining—namely that conventional learning rate decay schedules assign the smallest effective step sizes to the highest-quality data at the end of training, neutralizing the intended benefits of the curriculum.

Resolves a prominent puzzle in the literature: The findings convincingly explain why prior works on instance-level curriculum learning (e.g., Wettig et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2025) reported only marginal gains or even counterintuitive results when pairing curricula with standard aggressive cosine or WSD decay.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments systematically ablate decay lengths, ending learning rates, and checkpoint averaging strategies (EMA, SMA, WMA) across both pretraining from scratch (1.5B model / 30B tokens) and mid-training / continual pretraining (3.2B model / 150B tokens across multiple domains).

Principled and practical solutions: The proposed remedies—moderate LR decay (e.g., decaying to ~1/3 peak LR) and Curriculum Model Averaging (CMA/CDMA)—are computationally cheap, straightforward to implement, and leverage quality scores already computed in standard curation pipelines.

Theoretical support: The 2D stylized quadratic optimization model nicely formalizes the trade-off between progress along the signal direction and variance reduction in the noise direction, theoretically corroborating the empirical findings.
weaknesses: Pretraining scale relative to industrial frontiers: While 1.5B/30B tokens and 3.2B/150B tokens are solid for academic budgets, it remains an open question whether these dynamics hold identically over multi-trillion-token regimes where multiple epochs or dynamic replay buffers are standard.

Modest absolute gains in the standard from-scratch pretraining setup: In the single-domain from-scratch pretraining setup (Table 1), the absolute improvement of EMA+Ascend over WSD+Uniform is relatively modest (+0.39% overall average, +0.74% on Core tasks), although the gains become substantially more pronounced in mid-training (+1.20% avg, +2.21% Core).

Minor performance trade-offs on specific benchmarks: In the multi-domain continual pretraining experiment (Table 10), coding performance on MBPP experiences a slight regression (-0.78%), suggesting that domain-specific metrics (such as GitHub star counts) may need more refinement when integrating heterogeneous corpora.

strengths: Identifies a simple, elegant, and previously overlooked insight: instance-level curriculum learning (arranging data from low to high quality) places the highest-quality data at the end of pretraining, precisely where conventional learning rate schedules decay to near zero, thereby dampening gradient updates on the most valuable data.

Provides a convincing explanation for why past efforts on curriculum learning in LLM pretraining often yielded marginal or contradictory gains (e.g., reverse curricula sometimes matching standard curricula).

Proposes lightweight, practically deployable remedies—moderate learning rate decay and checkpoint weight averaging (EMA/SMA)—that co-design the optimization schedule with the data curriculum without adding computational overhead.

Solid empirical validation across multiple scales and settings: extensive experiments on 1.5B models trained over 30B tokens, ablation across scoring metrics (DCLM fastText, PreSelect) and datasets (WebOrganizer), and a large-scale 3.2B-parameter multi-domain continual pretraining run on over 150B tokens.

Includes both an intuitive river-valley loss landscape interpretation and a stylized 2D theoretical analysis that formalizes the signal-versus-noise accumulation trade-offs under different LR and data schedules.
weaknesses: The theoretical demonstration in Section 4 relies on a simplified 2D quadratic problem with fixed additive noise, which leaves a significant conceptual gap with the non-convex optimization dynamics of deep Transformer models.

While the average downstream improvements are consistent (+1.0% to +1.6%), gains on certain complex reasoning and coding benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K and MBPP in Table 10) are minimal or show minor regressions.
The optimal ending LR (e.g., approximately 1/3 of peak LR) and EMA parameters may require empirical re-tuning when transitioning to different model scales, batch sizes, or total token horizons.

strengths: Compelling and intuitive insight: The paper identifies a fundamental yet overlooked conflict in curriculum learning for LLMs—namely, that standard aggressive learning rate decay schedules (such as Cosine or WSD decaying near zero) implicitly de-weight the updates on high-quality samples placed at the end of training.

Solid and realistic academic evaluation: The empirical study is conducted at a substantial academic scale (1.5B parameter Qwen2.5-style architecture trained on 30B tokens) within the standardized DCLM framework and evaluated across multiple standard downstream benchmarks via OLMES.

Comprehensive exploration of remedies: The authors thoroughly investigate practical and elegant solutions, including tuning the final learning rate to a moderate value, replacing decay with checkpoint model averaging (CMA), and combining both (CDMA), demonstrating consistent benefits especially in practical mid-training configurations.

Sound theoretical toy model: The theoretical analysis on a 2D quadratic optimization problem effectively formalizes the intuition of signal-to-noise dynamics, explaining why aggressive decay truncates signal updates from high-quality data while weight averaging / moderate decay preserves progress along the signal direction.

Clear writing and practical utility: The paper is well-structured and written with clarity; the proposed fixes (CMA/CDMA) introduce negligible computational overhead and can be easily integrated into real-world pretraining and mid-training pipelines.
weaknesses: Compute and token budget scale: While 1.5B parameters on 30B tokens is solid for academic pretraining studies, it remains in a compute-limited / undertrained regime compared to production pretraining runs (which often train for trillions of tokens, far exceeding Chinchilla compute optimality). It remains open whether the observed curriculum dynamics persist identically at massive token-to-parameter ratios.

Moderate absolute gains in single-stage pretraining: In standard pretraining (Table 1), the downstream performance improvements over a tuned uniform baseline are relatively modest (~0.4% average, ~0.7% on core benchmarks), though gains become much more pronounced in the mid-training setting (Table 2).

Scalability of global dataset ordering: Sorting multi-terabyte or petabyte web corpora globally by quality metric incurs data-engineering overhead and potential distributed I/O shuffling bottlenecks, although the authors partially address this via stage-wise sorting (the A,A setting).

strengths: Identifies a timely, insightful, and previously overlooked phenomenon in LLM pretraining: the fundamental mismatch between ascending quality data curricula and aggressive learning rate decay schedules (such as standard cosine or WSD decaying to near-zero), which de-weights the most valuable data at the end of training.

Provides a simple, elegant, and computationally free remedy: using moderate LR decay (e.g., decaying to ~1/3 of the peak LR) and combining constant/moderate LR schedules with checkpoint weight averaging (EMA/SMA).

Solid empirical rigor: validations are carried out at a meaningful academic scale (1.5B parameters, 30B tokens) across multiple quality metrics (DCLM fastText, PreSelect), dataset mixtures (DCLM, WebOrganizer), and training settings (full pretraining and practical mid-training).

Provides both a clean intuitive landscape perspective (river-valley dynamics) and a formal 2D quadratic theoretical model demonstrating the convergence bounds under uniform, aggressive decay, moderate decay, and weight averaging regimes.
Careful experimental ablations that reconcile mixed and conflicting results in prior literature regarding curriculum learning and data folding strategies.
weaknesses: While the gains in the core reasoning benchmarks (MMLU, ARC, CSQA) and mid-training setups are noticeable (+1.2% to +2.2%), the overall average benchmark improvements in the standard pretraining setting (Table 1) are modest (~0.4% on average across 8 tasks).

Lack of multiple random seeds or error bars for the downstream evaluations, making it difficult to formally assess statistical significance, although this is somewhat understandable given the 30B-token pretraining computational budget.

The theoretical demonstration relies on a highly simplified 2D quadratic objective with linear SGD, which abstracts away key features of LLM optimization such as AdamW dynamics, adaptive momentum, and non-convex neural network landscape properties.

Global sorting across multi-trillion token datasets can introduce engineering and shuffle-overhead bottlenecks in production-scale pretraining pipelines, although the authors partially address this via their phase-wise sorting ablations.

strengths: Insightful problem identification: The paper identifies a fundamental and intuitive tension in LLM curriculum pretraining—namely, that sorting data in ascending quality places the best data at the end of training precisely when conventional learning rate decay schedules reduce update magnitudes to near zero, thus undermining the curriculum's potential.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The core claims are supported by systematic experiments on a 1.5B parameter architecture trained over 30B tokens, evaluating both validation loss curves and a standardized suite of 8 downstream evaluation benchmarks.

Practical and actionable solutions: The proposed remedies (moderating the ending learning rate in WSD schedules and applying Curriculum Model Averaging / CDMA) are practical, require minimal overhead, and yield clear improvements (+1.20% to +1.68% on average benchmarks in mid-training configurations).

Thorough ablations: The authors benchmark against alternative approaches such as stage-wise data folding, explore different checkpoint weighting mechanisms (EMA, SMA, WMA), evaluate multiple quality metrics (DCLM fastText, PreSelect), and test on an unfiltered dataset (WebOrganizer).
weaknesses: Limited pretraining token horizon: While 30B tokens on a 1.5B model provides a reasonable academic testbed, modern LLM pretraining operates in heavily overtrained regimes (hundreds or thousands of tokens per parameter, often 1T+ tokens). It remains unverified whether these curriculum effects and schedule trade-offs persist over much longer pretraining horizons.

Overly simplified theoretical framing: The theoretical analysis in Section 6 relies on a 2D quadratic objective with SGD. While helpful for basic intuition, it diverges significantly from the high-dimensional non-convex loss surfaces, adaptive moment estimation (AdamW), and complex feature dynamics present in transformer pretraining.

Modest absolute downstream gains in standard pretraining: In the single-dataset pretraining setup (Table 1), the downstream benchmark gain of CMA over the strongest baseline (Uniform + WSD) is relatively small (+0.38% to +0.39% average accuracy), with several individual tasks showing mixed or marginal differences.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: The optimal ending learning rate appears to be dataset- and curriculum-dependent (e.g., around 1/3 peak LR for DCLM, but zero decay performing better on WebOrganizer alone in Table 7), suggesting that users must still carefully tune the ending LR schedule.
